Check: F=2, G=6 (4 apart, yes), O=8, I=1 (O+1=I mod8? 8+1=1 mod8 yes), H=5 not next to F(2) or K(7) yes.  
✅ This works.

O and I: I=O+1.

Check H not next to F: H=2, F=4 → not next (good). H not next to K: H=2, K=3 → next! ❌ fails.

B) Ramos, Zane
C) Smith, Taj
D) Vogel, Zane
E) Yi, Zane
rationale: If Yi and Zane are both assigned to Labor, then the condition 'Yi and Zane must both be assigned to Pricing if either one of them is' is violated. Since neither is in Pricing, but the condition requires that if either is in Pricing then both must be, but here both are in Labor, so the condition is not triggered. However, the real issue is that if both are in Labor, then the Markets constraint (exactly 2 assistants) and the Smith-Taj constraint (same course) cannot be satisfied without violating the Vogel-Yi constraint (different courses) or the Yi-Zane condition. Specifically, if Yi and Zane are in Labor, then Pricing must have at least one assistant (since each course has at least one), but if any assistant other than Yi or Zane is in Pricing, then the Yi-Zane condition forces both Yi and Zane into Pricing, contradicting their assignment to Labor. Thus, E is impossible.

context: An economics department is assigning six teaching assistants—Ramos, Smith, Taj, Vogel, Yi, and Zane—to three courses—Labor, Markets, and Pricing. Each assistant will be assigned to exactly one course, and each course will have at least one assistant assigned to it. The assignment of assistants to courses is subject to the following conditions: Markets must have exactly two assistants assigned to it. Smith and Taj must be assigned to the same course as each other. Vogel and Yi cannot be assigned to the same course as each other. Yi and Zane must both be assigned to Pricing if either one of them is.
question: Which one of the following could be true?
options: A) Ramos and Vogel are both assigned to Markets.
B) Ramos and Taj are both assigned to Markets.
C) Smith and Vogel are both assigned to Markets.
D) Smith and Zane are both assigned to Pricing.
E) Vogel and Zane are both assigned to Pricing.
rationale: Option B is satisfiable: Markets has exactly two assistants (Smith and Taj, who must be together), and the constraints on Vogel, Yi, and Zane are not violated. The other options conflict with constraints: A violates Vogel-Yi separation if both are in Markets (since Yi would then be in Pricing alone, breaking the Yi-Zane condition), C forces Smith and Taj into Markets with Vogel, leaving Yi in Pricing alone (violating Yi-Zane), D and E violate the Yi-Zane condition by placing only one of them in Pricing.

question: If Vogel is assigned to the same course as Zane, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
options: A) Ramos is assigned to Labor.
B) Smith is assigned to Labor.
C) Taj is assigned to Markets.
D) Ramos is assigned to Pricing.
E) Smith is assigned to Pricing.
rationale: Given Vogel and Zane are in the same course, and Yi and Zane must both be in Pricing if either is, then Vogel cannot be in Pricing (since Vogel and Yi cannot be together). Thus, Vogel and Zane are in Labor or Markets. If Taj is in Markets, then Smith is also in Markets (since Smith and Taj are together). Markets then has Smith, Taj, and possibly Vogel and Zane, but Markets must have exactly two assistants. If Vogel and Zane are in Markets, that would make four assistants in Markets, violating the constraint. If Vogel and Zane are in Labor, then Markets has Smith and Taj (two assistants), but then Yi must be in Pricing (since Zane is not in Pricing, so Yi cannot be in Pricing unless Zane is also in Pricing — but Zane is in Labor, so Yi cannot be in Pricing). This forces Yi into Labor or Markets, but Labor already has Vogel and Zane, so Yi cannot join Labor (Vogel conflict), and Markets already has two assistants (Smith and Taj), so Yi cannot join Markets. This leaves no valid course for Yi, which is a contradiction. Therefore, Taj cannot be in Markets.

context: There are exactly six computers—P, Q, R, S, T, and U—on a small network. Exactly one of those computers was infected by a virus from outside the network, and that virus was then transmitted between computers on the network. Each computer received the virus exactly once. The following pieces of information concerning the spread of the virus have been established: No computer transmitted the virus to more than two other computers on the network. S transmitted the virus to exactly one other computer on the network. The computer that transmitted the virus to R also transmitted it to S. Either R or T transmitted the virus to Q. Either T or U transmitted the virus to P.
question: One possible route of the virus from the first computer in the network infected to Q is
options: A) from R to P to T to Q
B) from T to S to R to Q
C) from T to S to U to Q
D) from U to P to R to Q
E) from U to T to P to R to Q
rationale: The logic program constraints require that the computer that transmitted to R also transmitted to S, and S transmitted to exactly one other computer. Option B satisfies this with infected(T) transmitting to S and R, and S transmitting to one other computer (not R, since R already got it from T). Also, either R or T transmitted to Q, and here R transmits to Q. All constraints are consistent with this route.

question: Which one of the following could be the computer that was infected from outside the network?
options: A) P
B) Q
C) R
D) S
E) T
rationale: The constraints imply that the computer infected from outside must have no incoming transmissions and at least one outgoing transmission. Only R satisfies this in a consistent model: R can be the source (infected from outside), transmit to S (satisfying 'the computer that transmitted to R also transmitted to S' if R is the source, then R transmitted to S), and the other constraints (S transmits to exactly one, either R or T transmitted to Q, either T or U transmitted to P) can be satisfied without violating the 'no more than two transmissions' rule.

question: If T did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network, which one of the following must be true?
options: A) P transmitted the virus to S.
B) Q transmitted the virus to R.
C) U transmitted the virus to S.
D) P did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network.
E) R did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network.
rationale: Given T transmitted to no one, then from 'Either T or U transmitted to P', U must have transmitted to P. Also, from 'Either R or T transmitted to Q', R must have transmitted to Q. Since S transmitted to exactly one computer, and the transmitter to R also transmitted to S, that transmitter cannot be S itself. If R transmitted to Q, then R transmitted to at least one computer. But if R transmitted to more than one, it would violate the constraint that no computer transmitted to more than two. However, the key is: if R transmitted to Q and possibly another, but the transmitter to R also transmitted to S, and S transmitted to exactly one, then R cannot be the transmitter to S (because then S would have received from R and transmitted to one, but the transmitter to R is the same as to S, so if R transmitted to S, then R would be transmitting to itself, impossible). So R did not transmit to S. Since S transmitted to exactly one, and R did not transmit to S, the only remaining possibility consistent with constraints is that R did not transmit to any other computer besides Q. Thus, R did not transmit to any other computer.

rationale: Q cannot have transmitted the virus to two computers because it must have received the virus from either R or T, and the constraints require that each computer receives the virus exactly once. question: The spread of the virus among the computers is completely determined if which one of the following is true?
options: A) R transmitted the virus to Q.
B) T transmitted the virus to Q.
C) T transmitted the virus to S.
D) U transmitted the virus to P.
E) U transmitted the virus to R
rationale: The constraint 'The computer that transmitted the virus to R also transmitted it to S' means the same computer infected both R and S. If T transmitted to S (option C), then T also transmitted to R. Since S transmitted to exactly one other computer, T cannot be that one, so T must be the initial infector or an earlier node. This forces a unique transmission tree: T infects R and S; S infects one other (say U); R infects Q (since either R or T infects Q, but T already infects two, so R must infect Q); and U infects P (since either T or U infects P, but T is at max, so U infects P). This fully determines the transmission graph.

options: A) S transmitted the virus to T.
B) T transmitted the virus to P.
C) Q did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network.
D) R did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network.
E) U did not transmit the virus to any other computer on the network.
rationale: Given that P is the only computer that transmitted to two others, all others transmitted to exactly one. The constraints imply that the source of the virus transmitted to both R and S must be P (since S transmitted to only one, and P is the only one with two transmissions). Also, either T or U transmitted to P. If T transmitted to P, then T would have transmitted to one other (since P is the only one with two transmissions), but then T cannot be the source for R and S. Thus, U must have transmitted to P, and since U transmitted to only one computer (P), U did not transmit to any other computer.
